title: Object-Oriented Programming
description: OOP principles and practice in Java, updated for Java 21 (LTS).
resumo: Object = state (fields) + behavior (methods). Pillars: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction.
Encapsulation: private fields and methods that enforce the rules; an invalid value throws, it is never ignored.
A constructor leaves the object valid from the start; avoid empty constructor + setters.
An interface is a contract (a class implements many); an abstract class shares code (single inheritance).
Overloading: same name, different parameters (compile time). Overriding: a subclass replaces a method (runtime). Always `@Override`.
Prefer composition ("has a") to inheritance ("is a").
Polymorphism replaces if/else chains by type — the Strategy pattern.
A record is immutable and generates constructor, accessors (`name()`), equals, hashCode and toString.

subsections.subtitle: What Is Object-Oriented Programming?
subsections.formerSubtitle: O que é Programação Orientada a Objetos (POO)?
subsections.description: Data and behavior together, each object protecting its own rules.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** in procedural code the data sits in one place and the functions everywhere else. Any function can change any data, so a rule like "the balance is never negative" is checked in ten places — and forgotten in the eleventh.

**Concept:** object-oriented programming groups data and the behavior that works on it into objects. A class is the blueprint; an object is an instance of it with its own state. Objects collaborate by calling each other's methods, and each one guards its own rules.

**How it works:** the rule lives inside the class, in the method that changes the data. Callers ask the object to do something (`account.withdraw(50)`) instead of reaching into its data.
examples.interview_question: What is OOP and why is it so widely used in Java?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Writing classes that are only bags of data, with the logic outside them. The rule gets repeated in every service that touches the data, and nothing stops someone from skipping it.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** interviews always ask for the four pillars, but each one exists to solve a real problem in code that keeps changing.

**Concept:** Encapsulation: hide the state and expose operations. Inheritance: reuse and specialize an existing type. Polymorphism: the same call behaves according to the object's real type. Abstraction: depend on what something does, not on how it does it (interfaces, abstract classes).

**How it works:** in the example, `Shape` is the abstraction, each class keeps its fields private (encapsulation), `Square` specializes `Rectangle` (inheritance), and `shape.area()` runs the right version for each object (polymorphism).
examples.interview_question: What are the four pillars of OOP? Give an example of each.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Checking the type and deciding outside the object, instead of letting each type carry its behavior. Every new shape means editing this method. (With a sealed type, a pattern-matching `switch` is acceptable, because the compiler checks that every case is covered.)

subsections.subtitle: Constructors
subsections.description: Creating objects that are valid from the start.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a new `Order` with no customer or a negative total is invalid from the moment it exists, and the bug surfaces later, far away.

**Concept:** a constructor runs when `new` creates the object. It has the class name and no return type, and its job is to leave the object in a valid state. If a class declares no constructor, the compiler adds a no-argument one; declaring any constructor removes it. Fields not set get default values (0, false, null).

**How it works:** require the mandatory data as parameters and validate it before assigning. `this(...)` calls another constructor of the same class, so the validation stays in one place.
examples.interview_question: What is a constructor for, and what happens if a class does not declare one?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An empty constructor followed by setters. The object exists in an invalid state until every setter is called, and a forgotten one is not caught by the compiler.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** with a public `age` field, any code anywhere can set it to -5.

**Concept:** a getter reads a private field and a setter changes it — and can validate first. They are part of encapsulation: the class controls access and can change how it stores the data later without breaking callers.

**How it works:** add a getter when other classes need to read a value. Add a setter only when the value really changes after creation, and validate it. For business changes, a method named after the action (`deposit`, `cancel`) says more than a generic setter.
examples.interview_question: Why use getters and setters instead of public fields, and when should a class not have setters?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Generating a setter for every field. Anyone can change the id or set any balance, and the class loses control of its own rules.

subsections.subtitle: Abstract Class vs Interface
subsections.description: A contract, or a partial implementation.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** several payment methods share a contract (`pay`), and some of them also share code. Where does each part belong?

**Concept:** an interface is a contract: what a type can do. A class can implement many interfaces; methods are abstract by default, and since Java 8 an interface can also have `default` and `static` methods, but no instance state. An abstract class is a partial implementation: it can have fields, constructors, implemented and abstract methods, and a class extends only one. Neither can be instantiated.

**How it works:** default to interfaces for contracts — Spring injects dependencies by interface. Use an abstract class when subclasses share state and the same algorithm, with only some steps different (the Template Method pattern).
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface, and when do you use each?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An abstract class with only abstract methods. It is just a contract, but it uses up the single inheritance slot of every class that extends it. Make it an interface.

subsections.subtitle: Overloading vs Overriding
subsections.description: Same name, different parameters — or the same method, replaced.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** two different mechanisms with similar names, often confused in interviews and in code.

**Concept:** overloading is several methods with the same name and different parameter lists, in the same class; the compiler chooses by the argument types, at compile time. Overriding is a subclass replacing an inherited method with the same signature; the JVM chooses by the object's real type, at runtime. `@Override` asks the compiler to check that you are really overriding.

**How it works:** in the example, `print(5)` picks the `int` version when compiling. `a.sound()` runs the `Dog` version even though the variable type is `Animal`.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A signature that does not match the parent creates an overload by accident. The classic case is `equals(Order)` instead of `equals(Object)`: collections never call it. `@Override` turns this into a compile error.

subsections.subtitle: this and super
subsections.description: Referring to the current object and to the parent class.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a parameter with the same name as a field hides the field, and a subclass needs to run its parent's setup before its own.

**Concept:** `this` refers to the current object: `this.name` is the field, as opposed to the `name` parameter, and `this(...)` calls another constructor of the same class. `super` refers to the parent class: `super(...)` calls the parent constructor and must be the first statement; `super.method()` calls the parent's version of an overridden method.

**How it works:** a subclass constructor always calls a parent constructor — explicitly with `super(...)`, or implicitly the no-argument one.
examples.interview_question: What do this and super refer to, and when do you use each?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Forgetting `this.` in a constructor: `name = name` assigns the parameter to itself and the field stays null. Making the field `final` turns this bug into a compile error.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an inheritance tree keeps growing: `EmailNotifier`, `SmsNotifier`, `EmailRetryNotifier`, `SmsRetryNotifier`... every combination of features becomes a new class.

**Concept:** inheritance means "is a": the relationship is fixed at compile time and the subclass depends on its parent's internals. Composition means "has a": an object holds another and delegates work to it, so parts can be swapped and combined.

**How it works:** prefer composition. Inherit only when it is a real "is a" and the parent was designed to be extended. In the example, any channel can be combined with any number of attempts, without new classes.
examples.interview_question: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: One subclass per combination of features. Each new feature doubles the number of classes, and a change in the parent ripples through all of them.

subsections.subtitle: Immutability and Records
subsections.description: Objects that never change after creation.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an object shared by two parts of the code is changed by one of them, and the other sees its value change "by itself". With threads, it gets worse.

**Concept:** an immutable object cannot change after construction: `final` fields, no setters, and copies of any mutable input. It is safe to share, to cache and to use as a map key. A record (Java 16) declares an immutable data class in one line and generates the constructor, accessors (`amount()`, not `getAmount()`), `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. A compact constructor validates the data.

**How it works:** to "change" an immutable object, return a new one, the way `String` and `BigDecimal` do.
examples.interview_question: What makes an object immutable, and how do records help?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A record holding a mutable list. The record itself cannot be reassigned, but whoever created the list can still change it. Copy it into an immutable list in the compact constructor.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** shipping cost is calculated with an if/else per carrier. Every new carrier edits the same method and risks breaking the others.

**Concept:** each implementation of an interface carries its own rule, and the client depends only on the interface. New variations come in as new classes, without touching existing code (the Open/Closed principle). This is the Strategy pattern.

**How it works:** `Checkout` receives a `ShippingCost` and never asks which one it is. Adding a carrier means writing one new class; `Checkout` and the other carriers stay as they are.
examples.interview_question: How does polymorphism replace if/else chains by type?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A conditional that grows with every new variation. Each change edits — and can break — code that already works.

subsections.subtitle: Enums with Behavior
subsections.description: Enums are full classes in Java.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a status stored as a String or an int ("PAID", 2): typos compile, invalid values are accepted, and the rule "can this order be cancelled?" is scattered around the code.

**Concept:** an enum is a fixed, type-safe set of constants. In Java an enum is a class: it can have fields, a constructor and methods. It works with `switch` (exhaustive, no `default` needed) and with `EnumMap` and `EnumSet`.

**How it works:** put the rules that depend on the status into the enum itself, so they live in one place.
examples.interview_question: What advantages does an enum have over a list of constants?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Saving enums by position. JPA's default (`EnumType.ORDINAL`) stores 0, 1, 2...; add a constant in the middle and every saved row now means a different status. Save the name.
